title: telemetry-sla-decomposition-and-synthetic-workload-catalog-2026
author: Aisha Patel
body:
Summary

This document defines a telemetry-first approach to SLA decomposition for Redwood Private deployments and provides a catalog of synthetic workload definitions operators should run during acceptance, upgrade validation, and continuous guardrails. It ties high-level SLAs to concrete SLIs and metrics, specifies threshold guidance, and gives runbook steps and automation snippets for generating representative synthetic traffic.

Goals

- Make SLAs testable and observable with a minimal, consistent telemetry contract across private deployments.
- Provide a reusable catalog of synthetic workloads (light, burst, cold-start, KV-heavy, multi-tenant-mix) to validate throughput, tail latency, cache behavior, and fallback logic.
- Reduce finger-pointing by mapping metrics to ownership and runbooks for remediation.

Scope and audience

This page is intended for:
- Field operators and SREs running Redwood Private (VPC or on-prem) installations.
- Solutions engineers validating customer acceptance.
- Release engineers who must validate upgrades and rollbacks.

Instrumented surface and SLI mapping

We decompose the customer-visible SLA (e.g., 99.9% request success and p95 latency < 200ms for realtime text generation under steady state) into operator SLIs tied to instrumentation points. Each SLI below must be emitted as a time-series with the specified labels/tagging (tenant_id, model_variant, region_zone, node_pool, request_route).

SLI table (text table)

Metric | Purpose | Aggregation | Key labels | Alert window/threshold
-------|---------|-------------|------------|---------------------
request.success_rate | Availability as seen by client | sum(success)/sum(total) per 5m | tenant_id, route | 5m < 99.9%
request.latency_p95_ms | Tail latency for generation calls | p95 over 5m | model_variant, route | 5m p95 > 200ms
tokens.per_second | Throughput from runtime | sum(tokens)/s | model_variant, node_pool | 1m rolling drop > 25%
cpu.utilization | Node health proxy | avg | node_id, node_pool | 1m > 90% for 5m
kv.cache.hit_rate | Efficiency of KV/prefix cache | sum(hit)/sum(request) | tenant_id, model_variant | 15m < 70%
kvsnapshot.latency_ms | Snapshot/restore time for stateful ops | p90 | node_pool | p90 > 10s (warn)
queue.depth | Ingress queueing backlog | max | route, node_pool | > 50 concurrent requests (warn)
model.load.failures | Model load errors | count/1h | model_variant | > 1/hr (alert)

Notes: choose the tenant-visible success_rate and latency metrics as the primary indicators. All metrics should be tagged with the config revision and runtime version (labels: config_rev, runtime_semver).

Sampling and retention guidance

- Full sampling for request-level success and latency metrics for the active canary and production routes.
- 1:10 sampling for debug-level telemetry (layered traces) in steady state. Increase to 1:1 for on-demand diagnostics (see runbook).
- Minimum retention: 90 days for aggregated SLI windows (5m/1h), 30 days for traces.

Synthetic workload catalog (overview)

The synthetic catalog below is intended for automated execution by the operator harness (see examples). Each entry includes: intent, parameters, expected baseline metrics, and validation checks. Use the catalog in three phases: acceptance post-install, pre-upgrade validation, and periodic synthetic guardrails.

1) baseline-realtime-steady:
- Intent: Validate steady-state latency and throughput for a single-tenant, production-like request mix.
- Parameters: 100 concurrent virtual clients, token generation target 5–10 tokens/sec per client, model_variant: default-prod (e.g., gptr-13b-8q), sequence_len: 512
- Expected baseline: request.success_rate >= 99.95% over 10m, p95 latency < 180ms, tokens.per_second within +/-10% of the accepted profile
- Validation checks:
  1. no model.load.failures during run
  2. kv.cache.hit_rate >= 75%
  3. CPU utilization < 80% averaged across node_pool

2) burst-burstiness-sensitivity:
- Intent: Ensure autoscaling and admission controls handle sudden burst traffic without catastrophic queuing or head-of-line blocking.
- Parameters: ramp from 10->2000 concurrent clients in 90s, mix: 90% short-generation(64 tokens), 10% long-generation(1024 tokens)
- Expected baseline: request.success_rate >= 99.5% over 15m, queue.depth transient spike allowed but should recover to baseline within 5m

3) cold-start-cold-cache:
- Intent: Validate cold-start latency for model shards and KV-cache warmup behavior after a full service restart or node replacement.
- Parameters: 20 sequential model loads (different model variants), 50 clients sequentially hitting new prefixes to validate KV miss penalty
- Expected baseline: first-request p95 for model load path < 10s, subsequent requests p95 < 500ms, kv.cache.hit_rate rises above 60% within 10 minutes

4) kv-heavy-sync:
- Intent: Validate throughput and latency for workloads dominated by KV access (e.g., long-context retrieval).
- Parameters: 200 clients issuing requests with 10k-context lookups, small generation output (<=64 tokens)
- Expected baseline: kvsnapshot.latency_ms p90 < 150ms, tokens.per_second stable, no elevated model.load.failures

5) multi-tenant-even-split: (chaos-ready)
- Intent: Validate fairness and quotas across tenants under contention.
- Parameters: 50 tenants, each with 20 clients. Mix of model_variants and routes. Simulate one tenant spiking suddenly to 5x their baseline
- Validation checks: quota enforcement triggers for offending tenant, other tenants maintain request.success_rate >= 99.0%

Synthetic workload definition examples (automatable YAML-like snippet)

# Example job: baseline-realtime-steady
name: baseline-realtime-steady
run_duration: 10m
clients: 100
concurrency_per_client: 1
model_variant: gptr-13b-8q
sequence: 512
prompt_template: "Summarize the following text into 3 bullets: {{document}}"
traffic_mix:
  - type: generation
    percent: 100
    token_target: 6
validation:
  - metric: request.latency_p95_ms
    comparator: lt
    value: 180

Automation and orchestration recommendations

- Run synthetic jobs from a control plane host inside the customer VPC (can be the operator bastion); avoid external public runners to prevent egress variability.
- Use a Kubernetes Job or an ephemeral VM that has the operator synthetic harness. Persist job definitions as Git-backed artifacts in the customer repo.
- Collect telemetry to the local OTLP endpoint and to the Redwood observability aggregator when available. Tag synthetic jobs with test_id, run_id, and expected_profile to make them queryable.

Dashboards and queries (example ops queries)

- p95 latency for route X: "histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_duration_seconds_bucket{route=\"/generate\"}[5m])) by (le))"
- synthetic failure rate: "sum(rate(synthetic_request_total{test_id=~\"baseline.*\",status=\"error\"}[5m]))/sum(rate(synthetic_request_total{test_id=~\"baseline.*\"}[5m]))"

Runbook: Synthetic failure during acceptance

1) Confirm test metadata: get last synthetic run_id and correlate with control plane job.
2) Pull operator logs: kube logs or vm journal for the synthetic harness and for the runtime pods.
3) Check core SLIs: request.success_rate, request.latency_p95_ms, kv.cache.hit_rate. If success_rate < threshold, proceed to step 4.
4) If model.load.failures > 0: inspect model shards, disk errors, and model artifact integrity; if corruption suspected, pull artifact checksum and re-pull from S3-like store.
5) If queue.depth is high: increase admission control limit temporarily and scale node_pool, or trigger manual eviction of non-critical jobs.
6) If CPU or memory saturation: identify runaway process and restart affected runtime process. Escalate to runtime owners if rapid recovery not achieved within 10 minutes.
7) After remediation, re-run the synthetic job and validate. Document run_id and decisions in the incident ticket.

Pre-upgrade synthetic validation checklist (operator steps)

1. Snapshot config_rev and runtime_semver.
2. Run baseline-realtime-steady and burst-burstiness-sensitivity; capture golden run metrics.
3. Apply upgrade to a single canary node_pool.
4. Re-run the synthetic steady and burst tests against canary. Compare: p95 latency delta < 10% and success_rate delta < 0.1%.
5. If canary passes, proceed with incremental rollout. If canary fails, run rollback and open bug with runtime and scheduling teams.

Lightweight acceptance report template (paste into ticket)

- customer_env: <env_id>
- runtime_semver: <before> -> <after>
- tests_run: [baseline-realtime-steady, burst-burstiness-sensitivity]
- key_metrics_before: {"p95_ms": 145, "success_rate": 99.98}
- key_metrics_after: {"p95_ms": 152, "success_rate": 99.94}
- verdict: pass/warn/fail
- notes: remediation steps or follow-ups

Ownership and escalation

- Primary: Field SRE / customer-ops (owns running synthetic jobs and first-line remediation).
- Secondary: Serving runtime team (model load, kernel, kv cache issues).
- Tertiary: Platform infra (node_pool scaling, networking).

Appendices

A. Example synthetic harness CLI (pseudo)
redwood-synth run --job-file jobs/baseline-realtime-steady.yaml --output /tmp/synth-123.json --observability-endpoint http://otel.local:4318 --tags test_id=brs-2026-06-01

B. Example query snippets (PromQL)
- success rate: "sum(rate(request_success_total[5m])) / sum(rate(request_total[5m]))"
- tokens/sec: "sum(rate(tokens_emitted_total[1m]))"

C. Common failure signatures and likely causes
- High p95 but normal p50: indicates tail queuing (check queue.depth, threadpool starvation).
- Degraded kv.cache.hit_rate during synthetic: stale cache config, wrong prefix hashing, or network saturation to state backend.
- Model load spikes on restart: insufficient pre-warm configuration or too-conservative model residency policy.

D. Example synthetic job catalog index (short)
- baseline-realtime-steady: steady state profile
- burst-burstiness-sensitivity: burst ramp test
- cold-start-cold-cache: cold path validation
- kv-heavy-sync: KV-dominant workload
- multi-tenant-even-split: fairness and quota validation

Document maintenance

- Owner: Field SRE (Aisha Patel).
- Review cadence: quarterly or after any major runtime or scheduler change.
- Where to store artifacts: jobs/ directory in the private-deploy customer repo and a copy in Redwood test-bench repo.

If you need a runnable harness to start with, contact solutions-engineering@redwood-inference.com for the operator synthetic image and templates.
